note: Monotony: dull sameness, every day like the one before.
Exactions: hard demands that must be met.
Prosaic: dull and ordinary. Severity: harshness.
Eluded: escaped; he never managed to get it.
Easy to manage or control; willing to follow orders.

anchor: chief mate of a fine ship
note: The chief mate is the officer next in rank below the captain.

note: Pretences: false claims or appearances one puts on.
Impossible to describe exactly in words.
Unbridled: unrestrained, out of control, like a horse without a bridle.
Destroy completely, so that nothing is left.

note: The captain’s Scottish way of saying “perfect miracle.”

Abyss: a bottomless pit or gulf.
Lucid: clear-headed; able to think clearly again.
Not stirred up or excited by anything.
Shut in below deck, as hatches are “battened down” (fastened shut) in a storm.

note: Ruin and wreckage left by violent damage.
Twist the body about, as if in pain.
The ship’s officer who keeps the accounts and supplies.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Purser”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: A small armed warship, used on coasts and rivers.
A businessman paid to build a railway line.

anchor: held the doctor for an ass
note: Thought the doctor was a fool.

Tamil: one of the Tamil people of southern India and northern Sri Lanka.
Unwearied: never tiring or slackening.
British spelling of “pajamas,” loose clothes for sleeping.
Languor: a pleasant, sleepy heaviness or laziness.
Charming, as if by magic.
Fronds: the large divided leaves of palms or ferns.
A roadstead is sheltered water near a shore where ships anchor. A thoroughfare is a main route.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Road”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Islets: small islands. Garlanded: decorated as if with wreaths of flowers.
Festive, cheerful, like a celebration or holiday.
A pageant is a colourful public parade or show.
Directly: as soon as (British usage).
Calling: profession; here, other seamen.
Undefaced: unspoiled, not worn away.
Pirates, especially the sea-robbers of the Caribbean in the 1600s.

Merchant ships in the “country trade”: trade between ports within Asia and along India’s coasts, as opposed to voyages to and from Britain. Officers in this trade were usually Europeans; the ships themselves might belong to Asian or European owners.
source: Families in British India Society, “Country Sea Service”, https://wiki.fibis.org/w/Country_Sea_Service

note: Ships sailing on long voyages to and from Britain, as opposed to local Eastern trade.
Attuned: in harmony with; used to and suited to.
Unsteadily; in a way that could fall apart at any moment.
On the verge of: about to. Dismissal: being fired.
Engagement here means being hired for a job.
An easy job; something good for little effort.
Billet: a job or position.
Siam was the name of Thailand until 1939. Its king kept a modern navy in the late 1800s, and some of its officers were hired Europeans.
Lacking substance; not solid or real.
Disdain: the feeling that something is beneath you; scorn.
Took a job on a ship; a berth is a position aboard.

note: Very old; a common saying.
A water tank officially declared unfit for use.
Chartered: hired, so the Arab rented the ship for this voyage.

note: A person who has turned against his own country or side.

New South Wales was a British colony in southeastern Australia, with Sydney as its capital. It became a state of Australia when the colonies federated in 1901. The captain is a German who had settled there.

Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian leader who united Germany through wars between 1864 and 1871, told a parliamentary committee in 1862 that great questions are decided “by iron and blood.” A “blood-and-iron” air means a harsh, bullying manner.
source: German History in Documents and Images, “Excerpt from Bismarck’s ‘Blood and Iron’ Speech (1862)”, https://germanhistorydocs.org/en/from-vormaerz-to-prussian-dominance-1815-1866/excerpt-from-bismarcks-blood-and-iron-speech-1862

note: Steamers carried Muslim pilgrims from Southeast Asia across the Indian Ocean and up the Red Sea to Jeddah, the port for Mecca, to make the hajj, the pilgrimage every Muslim who is able should make once. The trade grew after the Suez Canal opened in 1869.

note: Steam up: with fires lit and boilers ready, so the engines can start.
Jetty: a landing pier built out into the water.

note: Toward the front (forward) and toward the back (aft) of the ship.

Narrow cracks and small hidden gaps.
Praus: fast Malay sailing boats. Coasting: sailing along the coast.

Pious: devoutly religious; done out of faith.

note: A landing place where ships tie up to load and unload.
Obliquely: at a slant, not straight across.
An area of water set aside where ships drop anchor.
Ranged close to: sailed close alongside. Ledge: a ridge of rock.
A name for God, used in prayer.
Begged earnestly and urgently for something.
Astern: behind the ship, in the direction of its back.

note: A lighthouse on iron legs screwed into the soft seabed of shallow water.

The long, narrow sea between northeast Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Ships from Asia entered it at its southern end to reach the ports of Arabia and, after 1869, the Suez Canal.
A dazzling brightness, like a blaze of light.
Thick and slow-moving, like syrup.
Amidships: in the middle part of the ship.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Amidships”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000
